questions.enonce_markdown:
5. (a) The following are components of an industrial system: **weaving; cloth; carpet; bleaching powder; dyeing; labour; land; bags; buildings; spinning machinery.**

(i) Arrange them under the headings: Inputs, Processes and Output. Tabulate your work.

[5 marks]

(ii) Explain Alfred Weber's Material Index concept.

[3 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) An industrial system (here, a textile factory).**

| Inputs | Processes | Output |
|---|---|---|
| Labour | Weaving | Cloth |
| Land | Dyeing | Carpet |
| Buildings | | Bags |
| Spinning machinery | | |
| Bleaching powder | | |

Inputs are what is put into the factory (labour, land, capital goods such as buildings and machinery, and the materials used, such as bleaching powder). Processes are the operations that change the inputs (weaving, dyeing). Outputs are the finished goods (cloth, carpet and bags).

**(ii) Weber's Material Index.** Alfred Weber, a German economist (1909), said that an industry is sited where its total costs, mainly transport costs, are lowest. He measured the pull of the raw materials with the **Material Index (MI)**:

$$
MI = \frac{\text{weight of the localised raw materials}}{\text{weight of the finished product}}
$$

Localised raw materials are found only in certain places (iron ore, copper ore, sugar cane); ubiquitous ones (like water or sand) are found everywhere and are left out.

- If **MI is greater than 1** the raw materials lose much weight in processing, so it is cheaper to put the factory **near the raw materials** (for example copper smelting, sugar and cement works).
- If **MI is less than 1** (the product is heavier than the localised materials, for example bottled drinks, where water is added), the factory is placed **near the market**.
- If **MI is about 1**, the factory may be anywhere between the two.

| Item | Answer on the map |
|---|---|
| (i) Area of low population density | The **Sahara Desert** (hot desert, almost no water). Other correct answers: Siberia, northern Canada, the Amazon forest, the interior of Australia, Greenland. |
| (ii) Named transport route | The **North Atlantic sea route** between western Europe and north-eastern North America (draw it as a line with arrows and name it). Other correct answers: the Suez Canal route, the Panama Canal route. |
| (iii) A fishing ground in the Northern Hemisphere | The **Grand Banks** off Newfoundland (north-west Atlantic). Other correct answers: the North Sea, the north-west Pacific off Japan. |

**Why these answers?** The Sahara has too little rain for farming, so few people live there. The North Atlantic route links two of the busiest industrial and trading regions of the world. The Grand Banks lie on a shallow continental shelf where the cold Labrador Current meets the warm Gulf Stream, which brings plankton and plentiful fish.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Briefly explain what you understand by the following:

(i) Conurbations;

(ii) Dormitory town.

[4 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) A conurbation** is a very large built-up area formed when several towns and cities grow outwards until they join together, so that there is no break of countryside between them. Examples: the Rhine-Ruhr region of Germany and Greater London.

**(ii) A dormitory (commuter) town** is a town on the edge of a big city in which many people live and sleep but go to work in the city every day (by road or rail), so it has few jobs of its own. It is mainly residential, with houses, schools and shops, but little industry.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) What problems are faced by the increasing world population on the use of non-renewable resources?

[2 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
1. **Faster depletion:** as the number of people and their needs grow, more coal, oil, natural gas and minerals are used, so these resources, which take millions of years to form and cannot be replaced, may run out sooner.
2. **Rising prices, shortages and damage to the environment:** as the easily mined deposits are used up, mining costs more, countries compete for the remaining supplies, and mining and burning of fuels cause pollution and global warming. This makes it necessary to conserve resources, recycle and develop renewable energy.
